ownership_reason: Only the gold sees each element at the moment it is inserted, together with the position it goes to: hop 1 sees only the list's size before and after, hop 2 hands over the collection's iterator, and hops 3 and 4 pass that iterator along. Once the gold has moved its position past an element the list declined, the next element sits one place too far right, which no caller can undo without rebuilding the list. The gold's javadoc promises that the inserted elements start at the given position in iterator order; on the trigger the one inserted element (4) lands at index 1 instead of 0. The convention is pinned outside the gold: the facade's javadoc ('Only elements that are not already in this list will be added, and duplicates from the specified collection will be ignored'); ListOrderedSet.addAll(int, Collection), the sibling indexed bulk insertion, tests contains(object) == false per element and moves its index only after an insertion, and TestListOrderedSet testListAddIndexed and TestListOrderedSet2 testListAddIndexed ([0, 1].addAll(1, [3, 0, 2]) gives [0, 3, 2, 1]) pass; ListOrderedSet.add(int, Object) and SetUniqueList.add(int, Object) insert only an element not yet held; TestSetUniqueList testFactory and testAddAll pin that repeated elements of the collection are ignored. Hops 1-4 are documented as passing their input on unchanged (hop 1 'The collection is passed on as given', hop 2 'Every element of the collection is passed on', hops 3 and 4 'The iterator is passed on as given'), so a hop that drops the elements the list already holds before the gold contradicts its own javadoc. The facade can do the same with one call, CollectionUtils.removeAll(new java.util.LinkedHashSet(coll), this), which passes the suite: that is the gold's omitted contains test moved up to the facade and applied to the whole collection at once (ListUtils.removeAll tests remove.contains per element), after which neither the gold's decision nor the receiver's decline in add(int, Object) fires; it is recorded as a bypass.
